name: Exemestane

lead: Exemestane (Aromasin) is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer. On looksmax.org, mostly teenagers discuss it for keeping growth plates open and adding height, often with growth hormone.
No trial has tested this in healthy adolescents. Users debate it against anastrozole and letrozole.

paras: It irreversibly inactivates aromatase, reducing oestrogen production, and is a steroid structurally related to androstenedione. Lower oestrogen is thought to delay growth-plate fusion.

The label lists bone density loss, hot flushes, fatigue, joint pain and fetal harm; a maculopathy report exists. Forum users report hair and hormone problems. Prescription-only; height use is off-label.

lead: Exemestane, sold as Aromasin, is an oral steroidal aromatase inhibitor that irreversibly inactivates the aromatase enzyme. The US label indicates it for adjuvant treatment of oestrogen-receptor-positive early breast cancer in postmenopausal women after two to three years of tamoxifen, and for advanced breast cancer progressing after tamoxifen.[1] It is a prescription medicine.

On looksmax.org it is discussed, often by self-described 15-year-olds, as an option to keep growth plates open for height gain, frequently alongside growth hormone, and as an alternative to anastrozole and letrozole.[2][3][4][5] Some users describe it as milder and as having androgenic properties; others report hair or hormonal problems.[6][7][8] No published trial in healthy adolescents testing exemestane for height or other appearance outcomes was found.
Label warnings include reductions in bone mineral density over time and fetal harm.[1] Case literature also describes bilateral maculopathy associated with exemestane.[9]

paras: The label's indications are described above.[1] The Intergroup Exemestane Study and an earlier randomised trial examined switching from tamoxifen to exemestane,[10][11] and Grokipedia reports a 24% relative reduction in recurrence or death in the former.[12] In premenopausal women, exemestane with ovarian suppression was compared with tamoxifen in the SOFT and TEXT trials, with long-term follow-up reported in 2023.[13][14][15] A trial of exemestane for breast cancer prevention in postmenopausal women has also been published.[16] Exemestane is combined with everolimus in advanced HR-positive, HER2-negative disease.[17]

Interest centres on height and on oestrogen control. Posters ask how to keep growth plates open until growth hormone can be obtained, or whether exemestane alone is worthwhile at 15; replies note that growth plates commonly close between 15 and 21 depending on puberty timing.[2][3] A comparison thread has a user stating that exemestane increases androgens, which they consider beneficial, and has a non-steroidal inhibitor recommended by another.[5] Thread titles claim that exemestane is androgenic and discuss voice pitch, oestrogen and body fat, though the excerpts are not available.[18][19]

The label reports hot flushes (21% versus 20% with tamoxifen), fatigue (16%), arthralgia (15%), headache, insomnia and increased sweating as the most common reactions in early breast cancer, with reductions in bone mineral density seen over time and a recommendation to assess vitamin D beforehand. It states that exemestane can cause fetal harm.[1] A 2025 JAMA Ophthalmology article describes exemestane-associated bilateral maculopathy.[9]
Forum threads include a report titled as exemestane having nuked someone's hair, and one titled as nuking oestrogen permanently; these are anecdotes and the excerpts were not available.[7][8]

Aromatase converts androgens to oestrogens; in postmenopausal women peripheral conversion is the main source of circulating oestrogen. Exemestane is an irreversible steroidal aromatase inactivator.[1] Grokipedia reports about 42% oral bioavailability, a half-life of about 24 hours and 85-95% oestrogen suppression in postmenopausal women.[12] Its structure is related to androstenedione, and a crystal-structure paper describes a related compound.[20]

Human trials are in breast cancer: the Intergroup Exemestane Study,[11] the 2004 randomised trial of exemestane after tamoxifen,[10] SOFT/TEXT in premenopausal women,[13][14][15] prevention in postmenopausal women,[16] and combination studies with everolimus.[17] Registered trials include exemestane in endometrial and prostate cancer.[21][22]
No studies of exemestane for height or other cosmetic aims in healthy people were found.

Threads cover where to buy exemestane, protocols, and use with growth hormone, and many are started by minors.[2][3][23][24] A poster who wanted to keep growth plates open says they took it after a doctor declined growth-plate surgery.[2] A reply in one thread states that non-steroidal inhibitors always win because the androgenic side effects of steroidal ones are mild.[5]

lore.intro: Exemestane is discussed as the gentler or more androgenic aromatase inhibitor for teenage heightmaxxing, with debate versus anastrozole.[2][5]
